system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta reduces striatal dopamine and produces bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and postural instability.
vignette: A 68-year-old man has progressive bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, a pill-rolling resting tremor, and reduced arm swing.
distractor_notes: Essential tremor is primarily an action/postural tremor without bradykinesia and rigidity.
Huntington disease causes chorea and behavioral/cognitive changes.
Cerebellar disease causes ataxia and intention tremor.
ALS causes mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs.
key_expl: Bradykinesia plus rigidity and resting tremor is classic Parkinson disease.
objective: Recognize Parkinson disease from its core motor features.

sources.title: Parkinson's Disease
sources.support: NINDS describes Parkinson disease as degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons causing bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor.

sources.title: Parkinson disease
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes cardinal motor symptoms of Parkinson disease.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Essential tremor is a common action/postural tremor syndrome involving cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuits and often improves transiently with alcohol.
vignette: A 61-year-old woman has a bilateral hand tremor that is most prominent while holding a cup or writing. There is no rigidity or bradykinesia.
distractor_notes: Parkinson tremor is usually resting and accompanied by bradykinesia/rigidity.
Cerebellar tremor is intention-predominant and usually accompanies ataxia.
Asterixis is a flapping negative myoclonus seen in metabolic encephalopathy.
Hemiballismus causes violent unilateral flinging movements.
key_expl: A bilateral action/postural hand tremor without parkinsonism is characteristic of essential tremor.
objective: Differentiate essential tremor from Parkinson tremor.

sources.title: Essential tremor
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes essential tremor as a common action tremor affecting hands and head.

sources.title: Tremor
sources.support: NINDS describes essential tremor and contrasts action with resting tremor patterns.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Autoimmune CNS demyelination produces neurologic deficits disseminated in time and space, including optic neuritis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, sensory deficits, and upper motor neuron signs.
vignette: A 29-year-old woman has prior painful monocular visual loss that resolved. Months later she develops leg numbness and spasticity. MRI shows multiple periventricular white-matter lesions.
distractor_notes: Neuromyelitis optica more often causes severe optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive myelitis with AQP4 antibodies.
Guillain-Barré is a peripheral demyelinating neuropathy with areflexia.
Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness without sensory or MRI white-matter lesions.
ALS causes motor neuron degeneration without sensory deficits.
key_expl: Relapsing CNS deficits separated in time and location with periventricular demyelinating lesions support MS.
objective: Recognize multiple sclerosis from dissemination in time and space.
clues: later spastic sensory syndrome with periventricular lesions

sources.title: Multiple Sclerosis
sources.support: NINDS describes relapsing CNS demyelination and characteristic neurologic symptoms.

sources.title: Multiple sclerosis
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes MS as CNS demyelinating disease with episodes affecting vision, sensation, and movement.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Acute immune-mediated peripheral nerve and root demyelination or axonal injury often follows infection and causes symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia.
vignette: A 34-year-old man develops progressive ascending weakness and absent reflexes 10 days after a diarrheal illness.
distractor_notes: MS is a CNS disorder with upper motor neuron signs.
Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness with preserved reflexes and no sensory symptoms.
Cord compression usually produces a sensory level and upper motor neuron findings below the lesion.
Botulism typically causes descending paralysis with cranial nerve involvement.
key_expl: Postinfectious ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia is classic Guillain-Barré syndrome.

sources.title: Guillain-Barré Syndrome
sources.support: NINDS describes acute immune-mediated peripheral neuropathy with ascending weakness and areflexia.

sources.title: Guillain-Barre syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes postinfectious progressive weakness and reflex loss.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors or related proteins reduce the safety factor for neuromuscular transmission and cause fatigable weakness.
vignette: A 31-year-old woman has ptosis and diplopia that worsen late in the day and improve after rest. Reflexes and sensation are normal.
lead: Which structure is primarily targeted in the most common form?
distractor_notes: Presynaptic calcium-channel antibodies cause Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
Skeletal-muscle sodium-channel defects cause periodic paralysis or myotonia syndromes.
D2 receptor signaling is not the primary NMJ lesion.
PMP22 abnormalities cause Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
key_expl: Most generalized myasthenia gravis is caused by antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors.
objective: Identify the postsynaptic target in myasthenia gravis.

sources.title: Myasthenia Gravis
sources.support: NINDS describes autoimmune impairment of acetylcholine receptor signaling causing fatigable weakness.

sources.title: Myasthenia gravis
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes ptosis, diplopia, and weakness that worsens with activity.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: PMP22 duplication causes inherited peripheral myelin dysfunction with slowly progressive distal weakness, pes cavus, and reduced reflexes.
vignette: A 17-year-old boy has slowly progressive distal leg weakness, high arches, hammer toes, and absent ankle reflexes. His father has similar findings.
lead: Which molecular abnormality is most likely?
distractors: Expansion of CAG repeats in HTT
distractor_notes: Dystrophin defects cause Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy.
HTT CAG expansion causes Huntington disease.
SMN1 loss causes spinal muscular atrophy.
MECP2 defects cause Rett syndrome.
key_expl: CMT1A is commonly caused by PMP22 duplication and demyelinating peripheral neuropathy.

sources.title: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes inherited distal peripheral neuropathy and foot deformities.

sources.title: PMP22 gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes PMP22 duplication as a common cause of CMT1A.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Anterior spinal artery infarction injures corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts while often sparing dorsal columns supplied by posterior spinal arteries.
vignette: After profound hypotension, a patient develops bilateral leg weakness and loss of pain and temperature below the lesion, but vibration and proprioception are preserved.
lead: Which vascular territory is most likely infarcted?
distractor_notes: Posterior spinal artery injury would preferentially affect dorsal columns.
PCA supplies posterior cerebral hemispheres.
ACA supplies medial cerebral cortex.
Middle meningeal artery is associated with epidural hematoma.
key_expl: Motor and pain-temperature loss with dorsal-column sparing is classic anterior spinal artery syndrome.
objective: Localize anterior spinal artery infarction using tract deficits.

sources.title: Spinal Cord Injury
sources.support: NINDS describes tract-specific spinal cord deficits after vascular or traumatic injury.

sources.title: Spinal cord diseases
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes vascular and other spinal cord disorders producing motor and sensory deficits.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Each cerebellar hemisphere coordinates ipsilateral limb movement through double-crossed pathways; lesions cause ipsilateral dysmetria, intention tremor, and ataxia.
vignette: A patient has a right cerebellar hemisphere infarct.
distractor_notes: Spastic hemiparesis is a corticospinal tract deficit.
Homonymous hemianopia is a retrochiasmal visual pathway deficit.
Isolated facial numbness localizes to trigeminal pathways.
Bilateral pain loss is not the typical cerebellar pattern.
key_expl: Cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral coordination deficits.

sources.title: Cerebellar Disorders
sources.support: NINDS describes cerebellar dysfunction causing ataxia and coordination deficits.

sources.title: Ataxia
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes impaired coordination from cerebellar and related disorders.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: CAG repeat expansion in HTT causes progressive degeneration of striatal neurons, especially caudate, producing chorea, psychiatric symptoms, and dementia.
vignette: A 43-year-old man develops irritability, involuntary dance-like movements, and progressive cognitive decline. His father had the same illness.
lead: Which brain structure undergoes prominent early atrophy?
distractor_notes: Substantia nigra degeneration causes Parkinson disease.
Hippocampal atrophy is common in Alzheimer disease but not the hallmark of Huntington disease.
Inferior olivary degeneration causes different movement syndromes.
Dorsal columns are spinal sensory tracts.
key_expl: Huntington disease prominently affects the caudate and other striatal structures.
objective: Connect Huntington disease with caudate degeneration.

sources.title: Huntington's disease
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes HTT CAG expansion with chorea and progressive neuropsychiatric decline.

sources.title: HTT gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes huntingtin and pathogenic CAG repeat expansion.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Alzheimer disease features extracellular beta-amyloid plaques and intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau neurofibrillary tangles with progressive synaptic and neuronal loss.
vignette: A 76-year-old woman has progressive episodic memory loss followed by impairment in language and daily functioning.
lead: Which pathologic protein abnormality is characteristic?
correct: Extracellular beta-amyloid and intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau
distractor_notes: Alpha-synuclein is prominent in Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia.
Prion protein causes transmissible spongiform encephalopathies.
Mutant huntingtin causes Huntington disease.
Dystrophin loss causes muscular dystrophy.
key_expl: Amyloid plaques and tau tangles are defining neuropathologic features of Alzheimer disease.

sources.title: Alzheimer's Disease
sources.support: NIA describes amyloid plaques and tau tangles in Alzheimer disease.

sources.title: Alzheimer disease
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes progressive memory and cognitive decline.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Absence seizures involve thalamocortical oscillations and cause brief staring spells with immediate recovery, classically associated with generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave activity.
vignette: An 8-year-old girl has dozens of daily 10-second staring spells with eyelid fluttering and immediate return to normal activity. EEG shows 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave discharges.
distractor_notes: Focal impaired-awareness seizures usually last longer and may have postictal confusion or automatisms.
Generalized tonic-clonic seizures include convulsions and postictal state.
Syncope is associated with loss of postural tone and hemodynamic triggers.
Daydreaming is interruptible and has no characteristic EEG pattern.
key_expl: Very brief frequent staring spells plus 3-Hz spike-and-wave EEG are classic absence seizures.

sources.title: Absence seizure
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes brief staring episodes and characteristic EEG findings.

sources.title: Epilepsy and Seizures
sources.support: NINDS describes generalized seizure types including absence seizures.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Sudden obstruction of aqueous humor outflow through the trabecular meshwork rapidly raises intraocular pressure, causing ocular pain, halos, headache, nausea, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil.
vignette: A 63-year-old woman develops sudden severe eye pain, headache, nausea, blurred vision with halos, a red eye, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil.
distractor_notes: Open-angle glaucoma is typically chronic and painless.
Optic neuritis causes painful eye movement and visual loss without marked red-eye pressure crisis.
Retinal detachment causes flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like field defect.
Conjunctivitis causes irritation and discharge but not fixed pupil or acute pressure symptoms.
key_expl: Acute painful red eye with halos, nausea, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil is a classic angle-closure emergency.

sources.title: Glaucoma
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes angle-closure glaucoma as an acute painful emergency with vision symptoms.

sources.title: Glaucoma
sources.support: NEI describes impaired aqueous drainage and acute angle-closure symptoms.
